title: Lesson 9 - A2.1 System Vulnerabilities
subject: Information Technology
bigQuestion: How can cyber vulnerabilities put an organisation at risk?

sections.heading: What is a vulnerability?
sections.text: A vulnerability is a weakness in a system that can be exploited by cybercriminals to gain unauthorised access.
points: Example: an organisation leaves software unpatched, so a known weakness stays open as a route into the network
One unpatched device can be the weak link an attacker uses to get in, spread malware or steal data
Network vulnerabilities: weaknesses in the technology and connections that make up a network
Organisational vulnerabilities: weaknesses in people, policies and processes

sections.heading: Network ports
sections.text: A port can be physical (such as USB) or logical, in software. Different ports are linked to different network services, and firewalls use ports to control incoming and outgoing connections.
points: 0–1023: well-known ports, for common network services
1024–49151: registered ports, used by specific applications or services
49152–65535: dynamic/private ports, for temporary or private connections

sections.heading: Firewalls and common network vulnerabilities
sections.text: A firewall is like a gate between a trusted network and the internet. It controls incoming and outgoing traffic, which moves through ports linked to particular services. A badly configured firewall can leave unwanted access open; good configuration reduces the routes an attacker can use.
points: Weak passwords and authentication
Outdated software
Unsecured network access points
Firewall misconfiguration
Phishing and social engineering
Insider threats
IoT vulnerabilities
No regular security audits

sections.heading: How attackers use open ports
points: They scan an IP address to find open ports
An open port can reveal which services and protocols are running
Port 80 (HTTP) is usually open, so malicious traffic can be disguised and sent through an expected port
Ports can be targeted in denial-of-service (DoS) attacks
Close ports that aren't needed, and configure the firewall properly

head: Vulnerability
The weakness
Risk and impact
Controls
rows: A weakness is found in software or an operating system, and the patch (fix) isn't installed
The known weakness stays open. One unpatched device becomes the weak link: attackers enter, spread malware, steal data or shut systems down
Install patches promptly; patch management policy
Portable storage can be lost or stolen, or misused by a malicious employee
Data copied or exposed; malware installed
Clear rules on who can use external devices; password protection, encryption, tracking and remote wiping

sections.heading: Poor access controls
sections.text: Access control decides who can access systems, files or data, and what they can do with them. A vulnerability occurs when the rules don't work properly.

head: Vulnerability
What happens
Example
rows: A user can access information or files they shouldn't
A student can see or edit another student's profile
Passwords are too easy to guess or crack
A normal user gets higher-level (e.g. admin) access without permission
A student account gains administrator rights
Changing part of a web address or request to reach someone else's data
Changing /profile/123 to /profile/124 shows another user's profile

points: Permissions: read (view), write (add or save), execute (run a program), modify/change (edit)
Give the right account type: user, admin, system or guest
Users should only have the access they need to do their job, no more

sections.heading: Organisational vulnerabilities
sections.text: Not every vulnerability is technical. Weaknesses inside an organisation can make attacks easier.
points: People: lack of training leads to mistakes such as clicking phishing links or sharing confidential information
Policies: unclear rules on passwords, software use or reporting suspicious activity leave data at risk
Process: poor permissions, or no incident response plan, make the damage worse when something goes wrong
Human-centric weaknesses: falling for social engineering, poor password hygiene, no security awareness training, misuse of access rights
Human error is one of the biggest causes of data breaches. Good training helps staff recognise threats and know what to report
Exam tip from the slides: poor training → unsafe action → possible data breach

head: Policy
Purpose
rows: Limits access to systems and data
Educates staff to reduce human error
Secures personal devices on the network

sections.heading: Passwords and incident response
points: A password policy should set sensible length rules, stop reuse across users or systems, ban obvious personal information like birthdays, manage inactive accounts, and give guidance on saved/autofill passwords
A password manager stores passwords in one place behind a single 'master' password
Password managers can be device-based (an encrypted vault), synchronised across a network, or cloud-based for remote working; they create complex passwords you don't need to remember
An incident response plan helps an organisation respond quickly to an attack. Without one, delays make the damage worse
The plan should be thorough and tested, so people know what to do when an incident happens

sections.heading: Exam method: the four-step chain
sections.text: Build stronger answers by linking four steps. Here's the slides' mini scenario (a school's old till system with unpatched software) done as an example:

head: Step
Ask
Example answer
rows: The school's till system runs old, unpatched software.
How could an attacker exploit it?
An attacker could use the known, unfixed weakness to get into the till and the school network.
What could happen to the organisation or data?
Card or payment data could be stolen, or the tills shut down, so the canteen can't take payments.
What control or policy would reduce the risk?
A patch management policy, so updates are installed promptly, or replacing the outdated till.

keyIdea: A vulnerability is a weakness attackers can exploit. Some are technical (open ports, misconfigured firewalls, unpatched software, USB drives, poor access control) and some are organisational (untrained people, unclear policies, no incident plan). In the exam, link Cause → Risk → Impact → Response.

o: A weakness in a system that can be exploited to gain unauthorised access
quiz.e: Vulnerabilities are weaknesses. Threats are what exploit them.

quiz.q: What is an open network port?
o: A USB port with nothing plugged in
A port that accepts connections, so a service can be reached through it
quiz.e: Open ports let traffic in to a service. Unneeded open ports give attackers routes in.

o: Software that hasn't had the fix for a known weakness installed
quiz.e: The patch exists but isn't installed, so the known weakness stays open.

o: Deciding who can access systems, files or data, and what they can do
quiz.e: Good access control means only authorised users reach the right resources.

quiz.q: Which is an organisational weakness that could help an attacker?
quiz.e: Untrained staff may click phishing links or share confidential information.

quiz.q: Which port is used for HTTPS (secure web traffic)?
Which port is used for DNS (domain name lookup)?
Why might attackers send malicious traffic through port 80?
o: Port 80 is usually open, so the traffic is disguised as normal web traffic
quiz.e: Using an expected port helps malicious traffic blend in.

quiz.q: A normal user manages to gain administrator access. What type of vulnerability is this?
quiz.e: Getting higher-level access without permission is privilege escalation.

quiz.q: Changing a URL from /profile/123 to /profile/124 shows another user's profile. What is this?
quiz.e: IDOR: changing part of a request to reach someone else's data.

quiz.q: A company lets all employees access every file. What vulnerability is this?
quiz.e: Users should only have the access they need. Otherwise one compromised account exposes everything.

quiz.q: A company has no plan for what to do after a cyber attack. What is the vulnerability?
quiz.e: Without a plan, delays make the damage worse.

quiz.q: Which policy keeps software up to date?
quiz.e: Patch management makes sure fixes are installed.

quiz.q: Which permission lets a user run a program?
quiz.e: Execute = run a program or process.

quiz.q: What are the four steps of the exam chain from the slides?
quiz.e: Cause (the vulnerability) → Risk (how exploited) → Impact (what happens) → Response (the fix).

apply.title: Name the vulnerability
apply.intro: Read each situation and pick the vulnerability or the best response. Then try saying the full Cause → Risk → Impact → Response chain out loud.

items.task: A security update was released three months ago, but the office PCs still haven't installed it.
items.e: The fix exists but isn't installed, so the known weakness is still open.

items.task: A student logs in and can edit other students' coursework files.
items.e: Users accessing files they shouldn't is broken access control.

items.task: An attacker scans a company's IP address and finds several unused ports open.
items.e: Unneeded open ports are routes in, so close them and configure the firewall properly.

items.task: A receptionist's account suddenly has full administrator rights it was never given.
items.e: A normal user gaining admin access without permission is privilege escalation.

items.task: An employee copies the customer database onto a USB stick and takes it home.
items.e: External storage can be misused to copy data. Use rules on device use, encryption and tracking.

items.task: Staff passwords include 'password123' and their birthdays.
items.e: Easily guessed passwords. A password policy and password manager help.

items.task: A ransomware attack hits, and nobody knows who to call or what to switch off. Recovery takes weeks.
items.e: Without a tested plan, delays make the damage worse.

items.task: Staff keep clicking links in fake emails because nobody has shown them what phishing looks like.
items.e: Poor training → unsafe action → possible data breach.

items.task: Staff connect their own phones and laptops to the company network with no rules at all. Which policy is missing?
items.e: A BYOD policy secures personal devices on the network.

items.task: A web address ends in /invoice/5001. A customer changes it to /invoice/5002 and sees someone else's invoice.
items.e: Changing part of a request to reach someone else's data is IDOR.

items.task: Which response best fixes unpatched software across a whole organisation?
items.e: Patch management keeps software up to date.

items.task: Which is the correct order for a strong exam answer?
items.e: Start with the vulnerability, then how it's exploited, what happens, and how to fix it.

exam.q: 2. State the port number normally used for HTTPS traffic.
exam.tip: Learn the port table: 21 FTP, 22 SSH, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS.

exam.q: 3. Explain how an attacker could exploit open network ports.
pts: The attacker scans the organisation's IP address to find open ports
Open ports reveal which services and protocols are running, showing possible ways in
so the attacker can target those services, disguise malicious traffic through an expected port (e.g. 80), or launch a DoS attack
exam.tip: Find → learn → attack. Three linked steps.

exam.q: 4. Explain the difference between broken access control and privilege escalation.
pts: Broken access control is when a user can access information or files they shouldn't be able to
whereas privilege escalation is when a normal user gains higher-level access, such as admin rights, without permission
exam.tip: Use the slides' examples: seeing another student's profile vs a student account gaining admin rights.

exam.q: 5. Describe two security policies an organisation could use to reduce vulnerabilities.
pts: Policy 1 named, e.g. patch management policy
Description, e.g. makes sure updates are installed promptly so software is kept up to date
Policy 2 named, e.g. password / access control / BYOD / incident response policy
Description, e.g. enforces strong passwords / limits access to what each user needs / secures personal devices / guides actions after an incident
exam.tip: Name it + say what it does. Nine policies are on your slides, so pick two you can describe clearly.

exam.sc: Hillside School's canteen uses an old till system that hasn't had software updates for two years. Every member of staff can open every file on the shared drive, including student records. Teachers often bring in their own USB sticks to move files. The school's firewall has several unused ports open, and there is no plan for what to do if the school suffers a cyber attack.
exam.q: 6. Using cause, risk, impact and response, explain the vulnerability created by Hillside School's canteen till.
pts: Cause: the till runs old software that hasn't been patched for two years
Risk: an attacker can exploit the known, unfixed weakness to get into the till and the school network
Impact: payment data could be stolen, malware spread, or the tills shut down so the canteen can't take payments
Response: a patch management policy so updates are installed, or replace the outdated till

exam.q: 7. Every member of staff at Hillside can open every file. Identify the vulnerability and explain why it is a risk.
pts: Vulnerability: poor access control (users have more access than they need)
If any one staff account is compromised, e.g. by phishing, the attacker can reach all files
so confidential student records could be viewed, changed or stolen, causing a data breach
exam.tip: Name the weakness, then follow the chain: risk → impact.

exam.q: 8. Hillside has no plan for what to do after a cyber attack. Explain one possible impact.
pts: Without an incident response plan, staff won't know what to do, so the response is delayed
which makes the damage worse, e.g. malware spreads further, more data is lost, and the school is disrupted for longer
exam.tip: From the plenary: no plan → delays → more damage.

exam.q: 9. Evaluate which security policy Hillside School should introduce first.
pts: Considers a patch management policy: fixes the unpatched till, a known route into the network
Considers an access control policy: limits who can open student records, reducing the impact of any breach
Considers a BYOD / external device policy: controls teachers' USB sticks, which could bring in malware or leak data
Considers an incident response policy and firewall configuration (closing unused ports)
Compares likelihood and impact, e.g. open ports and unpatched software are easy routes in; student records are highly sensitive
Justified conclusion: chooses one policy as most urgent, with a clear reason linked to Hillside
exam.tip: Top-grade "evaluate" = weigh up several policies against Hillside's actual weaknesses, then make a clear, justified choice.
